Beyond Preferences: Learning Alignment Principles Grounded in Human Reasons and Values

Henry Bell email: henry.bell@duke.edu Affiliation: Duke University, Durham, North Carolina, USA , Lara Neubauer da Costa Schertel email: lara.neubauerdacostaschertel@duke.edu Affiliation: Duke University, Durham, North Carolina, USA , Bochu Ding email: bochu.ding@duke.edu Affiliation: Duke University, Durham, North Carolina, USA and Brandon Fain email: btfain@cs.duke.edu Affiliation: Duke University, Durham, North Carolina, USA

A crucial consideration when developing and deploying Large Language Models (LLMs) is the human values to which these models are aligned. In the constitutional framework of alignment models are aligned to a set of principles (the constitution) specified in natural language. However, it is unclear how to fairly determine this constitution with widespread stakeholder input. In this work we propose Grounded Constitutional AI (GCAI), a unified framework for generating constitutions of principles that are representative of both users’ general expectations toward AI (general principles) and their interaction-time preferences (contextual principles). We extend the Inverse Constitutional AI (ICAI) approach to generate contextual principles from human preference annotation data by leveraging human-provided reasons for their preferences. We supplement these contextual principles with general principles surfaced from user statements of values regarding AI. We show that a constitution generated by GCAI is preferred by humans over one generated through ICAI both personally, and for widespread use in governing AI behavior. Additionally participants consider the GCAI constitution to be more morally grounded, coherent, and pluralistic.

1. Introduction

Aligning Large Language Models (LLMs) to human values has emerged as a critical challenge of modern ethical AI (Amodei et al., 2016; Gabriel, 2020; Christian, 2021; Askell et al., 2021; Ji et al., 2025). Constitutional alignment techniques (Bai et al., 2022b; Huang et al., 2024; Fränken et al., 2024; Findeis et al., 2025; Kyrychenko et al., 2025) align large language models (LLMs) to constitutions of principles specified in natural language (such as “respect human autonomy” or “do not use offensive language”). A natural question is which principles should we use? There is disagreement over values for alignment in a pluralistic society where LLMs are deployed in diverse contexts (Wu et al., 2023; Sorensen et al., 2024a; Gordon et al., 2022; Sorensen et al., 2024b; Conitzer et al., 2024). Rather than argue for a particular set of principles, we consider the question of a fair process for eliciting principles (Gabriel and Keeling, 2025) from stakeholder input (Freeman, 2010; Groves et al., 2023; Suresh et al., 2024; Huang et al., 2024). Deliberation (Huang et al., 2024) and social choice (Conitzer et al., 2024) have been proposed as possibilities for determining constitutions, but both methods require ways to elicit initial candidate principles–whether for seeding deliberation, voting, or both.

A critical challenge is scalability: How can we incorporate the input of potentially millions of stakeholders and distill their perspectives down to a reasonable number of candidate principles? Individuals may express thousands of diverse views, general or specific, redundant, conflicting, or overlapping. To address this need, we propose GCAI: Grounded Constitutional AI, a unified learning framework to elicit candidate alignment principles from stakeholder input. By learning we do not mean data collection. Rather, GCAI is a scalable unsupervised machine learning framework that can synthesize large volumes of human preference annotations with reasons and general human descriptions of AI alignment values into a compact set of representative candidate principles (a constitution).

Prior work has similarly attempted to learn principles purely from human preference annotations, a method coined as Inverse Constitutional AI (ICAI) (Findeis et al., 2025). We surface the need of further grounding principle learning using: (i) reasons (or justifications) for human preference annotations, written in natural language, and (ii) general values humans report for LLM alignment, also written in natural language. At a high level, GCAI works in four main steps, the details of which vary slightly between (i) and (ii) and are specified in Section 4 with full prompts available in the Appendix.

  1. (1)

    Candidate Generation. Using an LLM, we automatically rephrase individual reasons for preference annotations or general statements of values into one or more correctly formatted and generally applicable principles. This step is necessary as many human-written reasons or values are too narrow and specific (e.g., referring to a particular prompt), involve many semantically distinct concepts, or are simply written informally and idiomatically.

  2. (2)

    Clustering. We embed each candidate principle as a numerical vector using a sequence embedding model. We then cluster the resulting embedded candidates. Clustering serves two purposes: Deduplication of many repeated candidates and identification of broadly relevant themes.

  3. (3)

    Summarization. Using an LLM, we automatically summarize the most central candidates within each cluster (which often include somewhat different wordings of similar concepts) as new candidate principles.

  4. (4)

    Scoring and Selection. The reduced set of summarized candidates are scored, either by their ability to predict relevant preferences (for preference annotations with reasons) or by their centrality within the embedding space as a soft proxy for consensus (for general statements of values). The top scoring candidates (up to the desired number) are selected.

Outline and Contributions

  1. (1)

    Section 2 characterizes two kinds of principles: contextual and general. We argue that contextual principles should be grounded in reasons or justifications, and that general principles are also necessary to faithfully capture relevant value and concerns about alignment.

  2. (2)

    Section 3 surveys related work on alignment, principle elicitation, and evaluation criteria for constitutions.

  3. (3)

    Section 4 presents Grounded Constitutional AI (GCAI), the first unified framework for eliciting a constitution grounded in contextual and general human reasons and values written in natural language.

  4. (4)

    Section 5 discusses our evaluation methodology, including a discussion of the novel evaluation criteria we propose for constitutions.

  5. (5)

    Section 6 presents our main empirical results evaluating a constitution learned by GCAI compared to ICAI. Human survey participants overwhelmingly prefer the GCAI constitution across multiple evaluation dimensions, and we investigate the reasons for these preferences.

  6. (6)

    Section 7 presents qualitative and benchmark results of a model that we align to our the constitution learned by GCAI in comparison to that learned by ICAI. While the constitutions make little difference in benchmark performance, qualitatively we find that there are consistent thematic differences between the resulting models, with the GCAI-aligned model showing much more emphasis on ethics, safety, and non-discrimination.

  7. (7)

    Section 8 concludes with reflections on constitutional elicitation broadly based on our findings.

2. Grounding in Human Reasons and Values: Contextual and General Principles

We distinguish between two kinds of alignment principles the differ in their origin:

  • •

    Contextual principles arise from actual interaction experience with models. They may depend heavily on the prompt distribution, pretraining, and fine-tuning of the particular model with which a human interacts.

  • •

    General principles arise from anticipated concerns about hypothetical or possible model behavior. They represent prior commitments and do not depend on particular observed behaviors of a given LLM but rather on the broad values and concerns about possible LLM use.

Inverse Constitutional AI (ICAI) (Findeis et al., 2025) tries to learn constitutional principles directly from preference annotations, a characteristic source for contextual principles. A human preference annotation includes a prompt, two example responses, and a selection of the preferred response. However, we emphasize that principles are underdetermined by preference annotations, in the sense that a given preference annotation might be grounded in multiple unrelated or even conflicting reasons for that preference. For example, consider the following preference annotation drawn from the Helpsteer 2 Dataset (Wang et al., 2024).

The user prompt uses nonsense words, and both responses politely express a need for clarification and a willingness to help. What might explain the preference for Response 2? Multiple plausible reasons come to mind that would result in very different candidate principles. For example, perhaps Response 2 is preferred because it is more complete and detailed, fully clarifying its intended purpose and precisely highlighting the exact terms it cannot interpret. While initially plausible, this would completely miss the mark of the actual annotator reasons.

The actual reasons serve to ground principles of openness and non-dismissiveness in tone, having nothing to do with a preference for a more detailed response. An LLM (or human, for that matter) attempting to derive principles from the preference annotations alone might come to entirely the wrong conclusion based on a spurious inference.

Contextual principles are invaluable as a source of nuance about style, tone, and complex interpretations of helpfulness. But they are also insufficient. In particular, principles to which the model is already well aligned will not surface regularly in contextual interaction. In other words, contextual principle elicitation is heavily biased by the model and prompt distribution used for collecting the relevant preference data. Related, principles regarding safety and harm that are rarely relevant to normal interaction (but represent critical risks in rare interactions), will be underemphasized.

We find evidence for this concern empirically by a comparative analysis of themes in the PRISM dataset (Kirk et al., 2024) compared to the Helpsteer 2 Dataset (Wang et al., 2024). Specifically, we compare the human written reasons for preferences in the Helpsteer 2 dataset (the contextual case) with the general statements of alignment values contributed by human annotators in the PRISM survey data before and apart from their actual interactions with models (the general case).11 1 We analyze the survey data only, not the conversational data.

The full results are shown in Table 4 in Section 6.5. Annotations of reasons for preferences on the Helpsteer 2 dataset (contextual) heavily emphasize the directness of responses, focusing on immediate correct question-answering and helpfulness. On the other hand, broader questions of tone, fairness, and safety appeared much more frequently in PRISM (general) where respondents wrote descriptions about issues that rarely appears in actual LLM interactions. For example: “The most important core principles would be user privacy and prohibition of harmful or misleading content, as these are the most important principles for user safety…” (Kirk et al., 2024). Incorporating general principles from such data sources enables us to more faithfully capture these important stakeholder concerns.

3. Related Work

3.1. Alignment Techniques

Most alignment techniques directly fine-tune an LLM on a dataset of human feedback, typically human annotations of preference between paired examples of generations. Examples of such techniques include reinforcement learning from human feedback (RLHF) (Christiano et al., 2017; Stiennon et al., 2020; Ouyang et al., 2022; Bai et al., 2022a), Direct Preference Optimization (DPO) (Rafailov et al., 2023), and its generalizations Ψ\PsiPO (Azar et al., 2024) and GPO (Tang et al., 2024). Constitutional alignment (Bai et al., 2022b; Huang et al., 2024; Fränken et al., 2024; Findeis et al., 2025; Kyrychenko et al., 2025) differ by explicitly articulating a constitution: a set of principles expressed in natural language. The original Constitutional AI technique uses a combination of instruction-tuning, self-critique and revision, and reinforcement learning from AI feedback (RLAIF) to fine-tune a model given a constitution (Bai et al., 2022b). Alternative techniques include supervised fine-tuning with AI-generated examples (Sun et al., 2023) or conditional mutual information maximization (Fränken et al., 2024).

3.2. Alignment Goals and Learning from Stakeholder Input

Prior work has argued that the normative aspects of alignment should be confronted explicitly through a principle-based approach (Gabriel, 2020). Helpfulness, harmlessness, and honesty have emerged as leading contenders  (Askell et al., 2021; Bai et al., 2022a; Ouyang et al., 2022) but may be too general and in need of interpretation to adequately inform model alignment. At a more detailed level, there is substantive disagreement over the relevant values and principles for alignment in a pluralistic society (Wu et al., 2023; Sorensen et al., 2024b; Sorensen et al., 2024a). For this reason, some have argued to focus on a fair process for determining alignment goals rather than a particular fixed set of principles (Gabriel and Keeling, 2025). Constitutional AI is promising insofar as the principles written in natural language are directly used for model alignment. This enables transparency and collective participation (Groves et al., 2023; Suresh et al., 2024) in the alignment process apart from the provision of preference annotations for training black-box reward models. How then can we elicit constitutions from participating stakeholders?

Inverse Constitutional AI (ICAI) (Findeis et al., 2025) attempts to learn principles inferred from human preference annotations. ICAI uses an LLM to generate conjectural principles that could explain a preference annotation, then scores the resulting principles by their ability to broadly predict the preference dataset as a whole. In the language of GCAI, this amounts to learning contextual principles from preference annotations without reasons. Huang et al. (2024) proposed Collective Constitutional AI, wherein participants propose principles directly and then vote on a subset of the candidate principles (Huang et al., 2024). This approach focuses on general principles. In contrast, GCAI learns both general principles directly from human statements of values and contextual principles principles from preference annotations corroborated by human-written reasons or justifications for those preferences, disambiguating and reducing the reliance on conjectural LLM interpretation of preferences.

3.3. Evaluating Alignment Principles

Most alignment projects focus on human preference evaluation of the aligned model or automated benchmarks such as AlpacaEval (Dubois et al., 2024) or Arena-Hard-Auto (Li et al., 2024). While we do align models to our constitution and evaluate standard reasoning (Hendrycks et al., 2021b) and bias (Parrish et al., 2022) benchmarks, we also seek to directly evaluate the constitution or principles themselves that are the immediate output artifact of GCAI and related techniques like ICAI. We draw from a landscape of three distinct sources to identify evaluation dimensions: foundational political theory, contemporary constitutional design, and AI-specific constitutional evaluation. In particular, the principles outlined by legal philosopher Lon Fuller’s in his seminal The Morality of Law are incorporated into our criteria of Generality, Clarity, and Coherence (Fuller, 1969). We also draw upon John Rawl’s concept of Public Reason, in which he posits that a justifiable constitution must be acceptable to all over which it holds authority, to evaluate with respect to Fairness and Consensus (Larmore, 2002). We also consider contemporary frameworks for constitutional design, such as that proposed by Nworka and Hedling, particularly as they focus on applications, from which we draw the dimensions of Feasibility, Constancy, and Faithfulness (Nwokora, 2022), (Hedling, 2011). Finally, we turn to literature that examine constitutions specifically as they relate to artificial intelligence. Although Moral Grounding of constitutions is emphasized across scholarship, it is of particular emphasis in Mei and Broyde’s (Mei and Broyde, 2025) framework of covenantal authority as a touchstone for constitutional evaluation vis-à-vis artificial intelligence. We expand on these evaluative criteria in Section 5

4. Elicitation Process

The unified framework for eliciting contextual and general principles follows a five-stage structure: 1) Candidate generation, 2) Clustering, 3) Summarization, 4) Scoring and Selection. Figure 1 illustrates how certain stages employ different methods depending on the dataset. In this section, we outline the implementation of each stage for both contextual and general principle elicitation.

4.1. Candidate Generation

For the contextual principles, we use a subset of the HelpSteer2 (Wang et al., 2024) dataset. We then use the model gpt-4.1-mini-2025-04-14 and the prompt in Appendix C.1 to infer candidate principles from the justification text, as in the following example:

Prompt: I want you to act as an explainer and go in depth about a topic. Response 1: Sure, I can help. What topic would you like me to explain in depth? Response 2: Sure, I would be happy to help explain a topic in depth. What topic would you like me to explain? Some things to keep in mind as I am explaining a topic: I will use simple language and avoid technical jargon as much as possible; I will provide examples and analogies to help make the topic more relatable and understandable; I will break down complex concepts into smaller, more manageable pieces; and I will provide a clear and concise summary of the topic at the end. Let me know what topic you would like me to explain, and I will do my best to provide a thorough and understandable explanation. Preference justification: Response 2 is slightly better than Response 1. Helpfulness: Response 2 provides a more structured and detailed plan for explaining the topic, making it slightly more helpful than Response 1, which lacks specificity. Clarity: Response 2 presents a more coherent and clear outline of how the topic will be explained, reducing confusion. Generated principles: Provide a clear and detailed plan or outline to enhance helpfulness; use structured and specific information to improve clarity and reduce confusion.

This exemplifies how the justification adds context and value to the preference, allowing the LLM to extract or infer principles that better align with the reasons why the user preferred one response, rather than simply inferring them from the preference label alone.

For the general principles, we use the free-text answers from PRISM (Kirk et al., 2024) that answer the question of which set of principles stakeholders think AI should follow, independent of what task it is performing. These responses were not single isolated statements, but descriptions of values that often expressed multiple distinct principles. To obtain individual principle candidates, we decompose each constitution into a set of principles by feeding a structured prompt and few-shot examples to the gpt-4.1-2025-04-14 model (See §C.2). The resulting decompositions can be seen in the following example:

Stakeholder-Written Constitution: Be friendly and uplifting in conversation. Do not show me any vile or unethical responses. Remember past conversations and learn from them what I like and don’t like. Always be respectful. Decomposed principles: AI should be friendly and uplifting in conversation; AI should not provide vile or unethical responses; AI should remember past conversations and learn user preferences.

In this example, we can see that some values arise that would not likely be observed during the interaction of a user with a previously aligned LLM, given that such models are already tuned not to provide vile or unethical responses.

4.2. Clustering

The initial list of candidate principles is embedded using OpenAI’s text-embedding-3-small model22 2 The specific choice of embedding model is not critical, as any model with comparable semantic similarity performance would be suitable.. For contextual principles, we use hierarchical clustering to group similar embeddings based on cosine similarity. Compared to the kk-means clustering used in ICAI, hierarchical clustering better preserves unique principles, since kk-means requires the number of clusters KK to be fixed in advance. Because the true number of distinct principles generated in the first stage is unknown, specifying KK is difficult: if KK is too large, de-duplication is ineffective, and if KK is too small, unrelated principles are forced together. Hierarchical clustering instead allows us to specify a similarity threshold33 3 We found 0.420.42 to be appropriate in our experiments in the sequence embedding space, rather than a fixed number of clusters.

When principles originate from stakeholder-written constitutions, we instead apply proportionally fair clustering (Chen et al., 2019). In this setting, the objective is not only to remove redundancy but also to ensure that different value groups expressed in the data remain represented in the resulting set of clusters. Note that this is appropriate for the PRISM survey data where humans directly contribute constitutions and can be seen as represented by their contribution. By contrast, we do not recommend proportionally fair clustering for contextual principles because the distribution is strongly biased by the prompt distribution human annotators considered (i.e., as an annotator you may have been given prompts that did not reflect your most serious concerns).

The maximal number of clusters is chosen based on the assumption that each proportionally fair cluster should represent at least three data points, which is consistent with the fairness assumptions of the method while still allowing for a relatively fine-grained representation of human values. For each such cluster, the most central principle is selected as the one whose embedding lies closest to the cluster centroid, following the representative-selection procedure of (Chen et al., 2019). After clustering, we apply an initial de-duplication step using hierarchical clustering, as above, to merge clusters that are extremely similar in embedding space, reducing trivial redundancy while preserving proportional representation.

4.3. Summarization

To generate a list of de-duplicated principles, we prompt an LLM (gpt-4.1-2025-04-14) to summarize the central principles within each cluster. We compute the mean embedding of all principles in a cluster and select the five nearest principle embeddings, which are then summarized. This deviates from ICAI, where a single principle is randomly selected from each cluster. Candidate principles within a given cluster tend to focus on a central idea, with slight variation in their precise wording. Summarizing a subset of these principles helps to faithfully represent more of the values present in a cluster44 4 On the other hand, summarizing the entire cluster, for large clusters, resulted in some overly long principles which simply enumerated the details from the individual items within a cluster..

4.4. Scoring and Selection

During scoring for contextual principles we consider how accurately candidate principles predict the original preference annotations. For each candidate principle and each annotation (prompt, two responses, and a preference), we prompt an LLM to select the response that better conforms to the given principle, with the option to abstain when the principle is irrelevant. A principle’s accuracy is computed as the number of times it correctly predicts the human preference when relevant, divided by the total number of relevant annotations plus a smoothing factor α\alpha55 5 We use α=9\alpha=9, proportional to the dataset size, to penalize principles that are extremely rarely relevant..

This scoring procedure is not applicable to principles derived from stakeholder-written constitutions, since these are not grounded in response-level preference data and therefore cannot be evaluated by their ability to predict pairwise response choices.

Therefore, we instead compute a mean squared distance (MSD) score for each cluster and rank clusters by this score, which provides a notion of internal agreement within a cluster and thus serves as a proxy for consensus over the represented principle. Because some clusters may still express closely related concepts, we perform a final de-duplication step using hierarchical clustering66 6 We use a lower similarity threshold of 0.3 to conservatively merge only near-identical principles while retaining semantically distinct ones., merging semantically equivalent clusters and keeping the cluster with the lowest MSD as the representative.

Finally, we form a constitution by selecting the top K/2K/2 principles from each of the two elicitation sources, where KK is the desired size. For ease of evaluation we use a value K=10K=10 in our experiments, though in practice one may wish to use a much larger value of KK.

5. Evaluation

5.1. Replication of Baseline ICAI

We replicated the original ICAI algorithm to generate a baseline constitution to compare GCAI against. We updated the models to use the same model for principle generation (gpt-4.1-mini-2025-04-14) and embedding (text-embedding-3-small) as our method. We used the same data for both algorithms77 7 For responses without a majority vote, we followed the random tie-breaking the original ICAI used in for the alpaca farm dataset, and specified that the original ICAI algorithm generate 622 clusters, mirroring the number generated in the GCAI clustering. In addition, we configured the optional final clustering step in the ICAI method to generate an equal number of final principles to our process.

5.2. Evaluative Framework

Our framework for evaluation was informed by previous AI constitution research(Mei and Broyde, 2025), contemporary literature on constitutional design (Hedling, 2011; Nwokora, 2022), and foundational legal and political theory(Fuller, 1969; Larmore, 2002).

This framework is designed to engage in three distinct assessments: legitimacy, conceptual integrity, and applicability. The first set of criteria answers the meta-question, "Why should the system be bound by these rules?" as part of addressing the question of credibility and legitimacy. One source is its moral grounding, a foundational criterion that threads previous literature, both canonical and contemporary. For example, Lon Fuller notes in The Morality of Law that "legality is not a matter of form alone, but of fidelity to a moral enterprise." (Fuller, 1969) Moral grounding as an evaluative dimensions, thus, challenges whether principles and constitutions are anchored in moral traditions that inculcate values-driven standards.

Political philosopher John Rawls, in his concept of Public Reason (Larmore, 2002), argues that justifiable constitutions must also be acceptable to all of its constituents, a position we capture in the dimensions of fairness and consensus.

The criteria of generality, clarity, and coherence assess conceptual integrity, the logical and semantic quality of principles and constitutions. In other words, they pose the question, "Are the principles (and constitutions) well-designed to guide behavior?" Generality addresses whether principles bear adequate conceptual breadth for situational applications and offer an architecture for predictable decision-making. Clarity assesses whether a principle can be meaningfully interpreted; it counterweights generality in ensuring that abstractions still offer understandable instruction. Finally, coherence measures at a constitution level the assurance of cogency such that principles can co-exist without significant conflict.

Finally, this evaluative framework asks, "Do these standards hold water in real-world applications?" The prima facie criterion here is feasibility, which examines how principles might intersect with technological, social, and economic constraints. With AI safety in mind, we raise an additional test of faithfulness, taking into account how human- or machine-based actions may distort the intent of a principle for malicious purposes. Finally, this framework considers constancy, a resistance to temporal brittleness, which cautions against transient assumptions encoded into principles written today and anticipates how shifting contexts may invalidate principles in ways orthogonal to original moral intent, logic, and application.

5.3. Survey Methodology

We evaluated constitutions generated by both algorithms through two user surveys: 1) constitution-level, and 2) principle-level. 101 participants were recruited through the Prolific platform and randomly assigned the one of the two surveys. Our protocol was approved by our institutional review board (IRB) and all materials are included in Appendix F.

51 participants completed the constitution-level survey. These participants were shown both constitutions (in randomized order) (See Figure 2 and Figure 3 in Appendix A). We first asked participants to indicate which constitution they would prefer both 1) personally, and 2) for governing AI behavior for the U.S. population. After each of these questions we also asked participants to elaborate on what factors informed their preference in free text. Lastly, we asked participants to rate the constitutions along three dimensions: 1) moral grounding, 2) consensus, and 3) coherence on a 5-point Likert scale.

The remaining 50 participants completed the principle-level survey. Participants were randomly shown six individual principles, three from each of the two constitutions. First, they were asked if they personally agreed with the principle, and if the principle would be appropriate for governing AI behavior for the general U.S. population. They were then asked to evaluate each principle according to its: 1) moral grounding, 2) fairness, 3) generality, 4) clarity, 5) feasibility, 6) constancy, and 7) faithfulness. Participants indicated on a five-point Likert scale their level of agreement that the principle embodied each dimension.

5.4. Aligned Model Evaluation

We aligned a based pretrained Mistral-7B (Jiang et al., 2023) model to the principles from both the GCAI constitution and the ICAI constitution we generated. We used the Constitutional AI (CAI) (Bai et al., 2022b) framework using principle-guided critique, revision, and preference-based optimization. However, we used DPO (Rafailov et al., 2023) for the fine-tuning with AI-generated preference feedback, while (Bai et al., 2022b) used RLHF (see §B for full details).

For evaluating the aligned models, we sampled 100 red-teaming prompts from the Babelscape/ALERT (Tedeschi et al., 2024) dataset, and generated responses with both the ICAI and GCAI finetuned models (200 responses total). These responses were qualitatively analyzed by researchers to identify differences between the ICAI and GCAI finetuned models (See §5.5). We opted not to submit these generations to crowdworker survey participants out of ethical concern, as several of these red-teaming prompts are highly toxic and sensitive (See §G).

We also evaluate whether alignment to different constitutions has an effect on the models’ language understanding capabilities as well as their social biases. We benchmark on MMLU (Hendrycks et al., 2021a) to measure general multi-domain language understanding, and Social Bias BBQ (Parrish et al., 2022) to test whether models exhibit stereotyping under ambiguous and disambiguated social contexts (See §7.1).

5.5. Qualitative Data Analysis

We conducted qualitative data analysis of the free responses collected in the constitution survey, and the responses generated by our finetuned models. For both analyses researchers double coded a sample of responses (38 and 32 for the constitution survey and finetuned model generations, respectively) to establish an initial code book. Researchers then met to resolve any disagreements between their code books and consolidate a single set of agreed upon themes. The remaining data was then coded individually by researchers. No new themes emerged in the constitution survey data, however three new themes emerged while coding the finetuned model generations. Researchers recoded all previous responses to consider the new themes as they emerged (See §6.1, and §7.2).

6. Constitution Comparison

We asked participants to compare the constitution generated by GCAI to the one generated by ICAI and evaluate it according to its moral grounding, consensus, and coherence.

6.1. Participants Preferred GCAI on All Dimensions:

Across all of our evaluation dimensions participants expressed a distinct preference for the constitution generated with GCAI over one generated with ICAI (See Table 2).

6.2. Factuality Informs Participants’ Preferences:

Our qualitative analysis reveals that factuality most often informed participants’ preferences between the constitutions. This code was present in 19 (37%) of personal preference responses and 18 (35%) of governing preference responses. When explaining their personal preference for the GCAI constitution, one participant said the following:

“Rampant misinformation is already a major problem in the US. [GCAI] is the only one that addresses the [issue of] false or harmful information.”

6.3. Participants Prefer GCAI for its Focus on Safety, Ethics and Fairness:

Across both the personal and governance preference questions (102 total responses) all 70 responses that mentioned valuing safety, ethics, or fairness preferred the constitution generated by GCAI. One participant noted that the ICAI constitution puts a greater emphasis on stylistic principles, while the GCAI constitution is more based in ethics:

“[GCAI] seems to be more ethically based, while [ICAI] is more focused on style… Clarity is covered in [GCAI]; ethical reporting is not covered in [ICAI].”

6.4. Participants who Preferred ICAI Focused on Direct Responses and Clarity of the Constitution:

Across both preference questions 20 responses preferred the ICAI constitution. Of these, 10 explained that they expected the ICAI constitution to encourage model responses to be direct, providing them only the information that they requested. 5 noted that they preferred the ICAI constitution because it was more concise, or easier to interpret. The remaining participants who preferred the ICAI constitution justified this preference through their dislike of the safety (2 responses), fairness (1 response) and tone (4 responses) elements of the GCAI constitution.

6.5. Participant Preferences Match Dataset Characteristics

The ICAI principles are all contextual, learned from preference annotations in the Helpsteer 2 Dataset (Wang et al., 2024), whereas the GCAI constitution includes general principles learned from survey data of AI alignment values in the PRISM dataset (Kirk et al., 2024).88 8 We analyze the survey data only, not the conversational data. We counted the frequency with the surfaced themes (Table 3) appeared in the datasets themselves. We used an expanded list of related keywords for each theme (See §D) and count the frequency with which at least one of the keywords for a given theme appears in a human annotator record. The results are shown in Table 4.

Annotations of reasons for preferences on the Helpsteer 2 dataset (contextual) heavily emphasize the directness of responses, focusing on immediate correct question-answering and helpfulness. On the other hand, broader questions of tone, fairness, and safety appeared much more frequently in PRISM (general) where respondents wrote descriptions about issues that rarely appears in actual LLM interactions.

6.6. Participants Expressed Little Preference when Viewing Principles Individually

We employed bootstrapping on the data collected from our principle-level survey. We sampled 10,000 participant responses, with replacement, to generate a dataset of participant evaluation scores. We used these scores to create confidence intervals for 1) Evaluation dimension means by constitution: the average scores for each evaluation dimension, collapsed across all principles in a constitution and 2) principle-level means: the average scores for each evaluation dimension-principle pair. We also computed a composite score for each principle collapsed across evaluative dimensions. These metrics, respectively, measure differences in 1) inter-constitution and 2) cross-principle performance.

When participants evaluated principles individually, there was no statistically significant difference in personal or governance preference, or for six of the seven evaluative dimensions between the GCAI and ICAI principles.

We also calculated the mean scores for all 20 principles (both by evaluation dimension, and collapsed across dimensions), available in Appendix E. Notably, despite being an important factor in constitution-level preference decisions (See §6.1), factuality was ranked 10th out of the 20 principles we evaluated.

7. Model Comparison

7.1. Benchmark Evaluation

We ran standard benchmark evaluations for factual reasoning (MMLU (Hendrycks et al., 2021b)) and bias (BBQ (Parrish et al., 2022) on both of the aligned models.

7.1.1. MMLU

Table 6 shows that GCAI and ICAI perform similarly across all MMLU domains. Overall accuracy differs by only 0.33 percentage points, which is within the reported standard error of ±0.0038\pm 0.0038. The same pattern holds for all domain groups, in every case, the differences are smaller than the corresponding uncertainty estimates, indicating no statistically meaningful difference in factual knowledge or reasoning performance between the two aligned models.

7.1.2. BBQ

Table 7 reports accuracy and bias metrics on the BBQ benchmark. Both models show very similar behavior. Overall accuracy differs by 0.34 percentage points, while ambiguous and disambiguated accuracies differ by less than 1.2 percentage points. Likewise, the bias metrics are nearly indistinguishable: for ambiguous contexts, the bias scores differ by only 0.0012, and for disambiguated contexts by 0.0021, corresponding to differences below 0.5 percentage points.

7.2. Qualitative Results

Table 8 reports the proportion of responses in which each theme was assigned for outputs produced by the GCAI and ICAI finetuned models. Although both models were evaluated on the same set of prompts, their qualitative response profiles differ substantially across several dimensions. GCAI is more frequently associated with safety- and norm-oriented categories, including harm reduction or redirection, ethical prompting, harmless resources and advice, and physical or mental health and safety. It also shows higher rates of anti-discrimination and anti-misinformation framing. In contrast, ICAI is more often coded as producing harmful or violent suggestions, mis- or disinformation and discriminatory content.

8. Discussion

8.1. Constitutions Are More Than The Sum of Their Parts

When evaluating standalone principles from the GCAI and ICAI constitutions, participants expressed little preference for principles from one constitution over the other (See §6.6). This was not the case when participants viewed the constitutions holistically. In a head-to-head comparison of constitutions, participants preferred the GCAI constitutions on all evaluation dimensions (See §6.1). This highlights an underappreciated dynamic of constitutions for AI alignment: that the synergistic composition of a constitution is an important factor in it’s approval from stakeholders. To further illustrate this point, we note that while factuality was the most important factor in making constitution-level preferences (See 3), it was evaluated similarly to other principles in the principle-level evaluation (See 14).

8.2. Constitutions from GCAI Are Only Candidates and Should Be Discussed and Ratified

GCAI is notably a framework for eliciting candidate constitutions from stakeholder reasons and values. GCAI is designed to generate constitutions grounded in the values of a stakeholder population, which could reasonably garner widespread support. While the GCAI framework employs various scoring metrics during final principle selection, these metrics are far removed from direct human input, and are applied to principles that stakeholders have never actually seen. These scoring metrics should not be interpreted as valid expressions of support from stakeholders. Crucially GCAI does not have a method for ratifying the constitutions it generates. Before employing a GCAI constitution for model alignment developers should verify with relevant stakeholders that the constitution accurately reflects the pluralistic values of the population.

8.3. Justifications Increase Transparency and Faithfulness

One of the benefits described in standard ICAI(Findeis et al., 2025) is the ability to better interpret the principles guiding a preference annotation dataset. By incorporating justifications into our principle generation pipeline we further increase the transparency of preference data by more faithfully adhering to the true underlying reasoning of the human annotators. One limitation described by the original ICAI authors is that multiple constitutions may explain data equally well, so ICAI cannot claim to surface the exact principles used by the original data annotators. While this remains a limitation of our approach (and is, we believe, an inherent limitation in inferring principles from annotation data) we believe that incorporating justifications allows GCAI to more closely reflect the principles used during the original annotation task.

Limitations and Future Work

In this work we combine human reasons and values data from two different datasets. In practice GCAI is meant to elicit both general and contextual principles from the same stakeholder population. Future work should validate GCAI in more realistic deployment settings with a unified data source and large scale deployment for testing.

LLMs are used for generation and summarization within GCAI. While grounding candidate in the justifications and values written explicitly improves faithfulness, GCAI cannot guarantee perfect faithfulness and is subject to any biases of the LLM used within the technique.

Additionally, while GCAI generates constitutions of principles, the technique itself does not automatically guarantee the appropriateness of every principle that may be generated. In addition, no technique can guarantee perfect representation of every input perspective when multiple stakeholders disagree. Thus the final results require human oversight. As importantly, the final results require discussion and ratification from the relevant stakeholders for any given deployment. Future work should 1) investigate stakeholder attitudes towards GCAI constitutions, and 2) formalize a fair ratification process that incorporates feedback from the entire stakeholder population.

Appendix B Alignment Procedure

B.1. Supervised Learning Dataset Construction

The dataset creation follows the same methodology introduced in CAI (Bai et al., 2022b). First, 2000 prompts were sampled from the Babelscape/ALERT (Tedeschi et al., 2024) dataset, which is specifically designed to elicit undesirable or unsafe behavior. These prompts form the basis for generating initial model responses that the model later critiques and revises.

For the generation of the critiques and revision, the model mistral-instruct-v0.1 was selected. This model is instruction-tuned but does not contain excessive safety layers or restrictive guardrails, which makes it similar to the model used in CAI (Bai et al., 2022b), a model that is primarily helpful, rather than strongly safety-constrained.

Given a prompt, an initial response is generated using the model, after which a randomly selected principle from the constitution is applied. The procedure consists of three stages: (1) generating an initial answer, (2) generating a critique conditioned on a principle, and (3) producing a revised answer. The following prompt templates were used.

B.1.1. Initial Answer Template

You are a helpful assistant. Provide your best safe answer.
User request: {prompt}
Assistant answer: {response}

B.1.2. Critique Template

You are a critique assistant applying the following constitutional principle to evaluate the prior answer.
Principle: {principle}
Task: Identify issues with the answer relative to this principle. Be concise but specific.
Return JSON with keys: rationale, required_changes (list of short bullets).
Answer to critique: {answer}
JSON:

B.1.3. Revision Template

You are a reviser. Improve the assistant’s answer using ONLY the specific critique below.
Critique JSON: {critique_json}
User request: {prompt}
Original answer: {answer}
Write a revised answer that addresses the critique while refusing unsafe requests. Keep it short and clear.
Do not reference the initial answer directly.
Revised answer:

Supervised fine tuning used a dataset composed of the initial prompt and revised answer to align a mistral-v0.1 model. The hyperparameters used are summarized in Table 10.

B.2. Generating AI Preference Data

Following the CAI methodology, we sampled 4000 prompts from Babelscape/ALERT, and used the supervised model mistral-sft to generate two candidate responses for each prompt in order to elicit meaningful diversity. The two responses were generated using different sampling temperatures, with TEMP_A=0.6\text{TEMP\_A}=0.6 and TEMP_B=0.9\text{TEMP\_B}=0.9, while keeping TOP_P=0.95\text{TOP\_P}=0.95 fixed, to further encourage response diversity. A gpt-4.1-mini-2025-04-14 model is used as a judge in order to determine which answer better aligns with a randomly selected principle from the constitution. The comparison process follows the structure introduced in the CAI paper:

B.2.1. Preference Data Template


Consider the following conversation between a human and an assistant.
The goal is to evaluate which assistant response better aligns with a specific guiding principle.
[HUMAN/ASSISTANT CONVERSATION]
[HUMAN] {prompt}
[ASSISTANT A] {respA}
[ASSISTANT B] {respB}
[PRINCIPLE FOR MULTIPLE CHOICE EVALUATION]
{principle}
Options:
  (A) [RESPONSE A]
  (B) [RESPONSE B]
The answer is:

Each generated comparison is stored as a (prompt,response_A,response_B,preferred)(\text{prompt},\text{response\_A},\text{response\_B},\text{preferred}) tuple, forming a preference dataset for Direct Preference Optimization (DPO). For the DPO preference data generation, the GPT model was not able to decide between response A or B in 24 cases for GCAI and 26 cases for ICAI. This results in a final preference dataset of 3976 examples for GCAI and 3974 for ICAI.

B.3. Direct Preference Optimization

DPO (Rafailov et al., 2023) is then applied to align the mistral-sft model using the preference pairs collected above. The supervised model acts as the initialization point, while DPO directly optimizes likelihood ratios to increase the probability of preferred responses relative to their disfavored alternatives. A crucial consideration when developing and deploying Large Language Models (LLMs) is the human values to which these models are aligned. In the constitutional framework of alignment models are aligned to a set of principles (the constitution) specified in natural language. However, it is unclear how to fairly determine this constitution with widespread stakeholder input. In this work we propose Grounded Constitutional AI (GCAI), a unified framework for generating constitutions of principles that are representative of both users’ general expectations toward AI (general principles) and their interaction-time preferences (contextual principles). We extend the Inverse Constitutional AI (ICAI) approach to generate contextual principles from human preference annotation data by leveraging human-provided reasons for their preferences. We supplement these contextual principles with general principles surfaced from user statements of values regarding AI. We show that a constitution generated by GCAI is preferred by humans over one generated through ICAI both personally, and for widespread use in governing AI behavior. Additionally participants consider the GCAI constitution to be more morally grounded, coherent, and pluralistic.
1. Introduction
Aligning Large Language Models (LLMs) to human values has emerged as a critical challenge of modern ethical AI ( Amodei et al., 2016 ; Gabriel, 2020 ; Christian, 2021 ; Askell et al., 2021 ; Ji et al., 2025 ) . Constitutional alignment techniques ( Bai et al., 2022b ; Huang et al., 2024 ; Fränken et al., 2024 ; Findeis et al., 2025 ; Kyrychenko et al., 2025 ) align large language models (LLMs) to constitutions of principles specified in natural language (such as “respect human autonomy” or “do not use offensive language”). A natural question is which principles should we use? There is disagreement over values for alignment in a pluralistic society where LLMs are deployed in diverse contexts ( Wu et al., 2023 ; Sorensen et al., 2024a ; Gordon et al., 2022 ; Sorensen et al., 2024b ; Conitzer et al., 2024 ) . Rather than argue for a particular set of principles, we consider the question of a fair process for eliciting principles ( Gabriel and Keeling, 2025 ) from stakeholder input ( Freeman, 2010 ; Groves et al., 2023 ; Suresh et al., 2024 ; Huang et al., 2024 ) . Deliberation ( Huang et al., 2024 ) and social choice ( Conitzer et al., 2024 ) have been proposed as possibilities for determining constitutions, but both methods require ways to elicit initial candidate principles–whether for seeding deliberation, voting, or both.
A critical challenge is scalability: How can we incorporate the input of potentially millions of stakeholders and distill their perspectives down to a reasonable number of candidate principles? Individuals may express thousands of diverse views, general or specific, redundant, conflicting, or overlapping. To address this need, we propose GCAI : Grounded Constitutional AI , a unified learning framework to elicit candidate alignment principles from stakeholder input. By learning we do not mean data collection. Rather, GCAI is a scalable unsupervised machine learning framework that can synthesize large volumes of human preference annotations with reasons and general human descriptions of AI alignment values into a compact set of representative candidate principles (a constitution).
Prior work has similarly attempted to learn principles purely from human preference annotations, a method coined as Inverse Constitutional AI (ICAI) ( Findeis et al., 2025 ) . We surface the need of further grounding principle learning using: (i) reasons (or justifications) for human preference annotations, written in natural language, and (ii) general values humans report for LLM alignment, also written in natural language. At a high level, GCAI works in four main steps, the details of which vary slightly between (i) and (ii) and are specified in Section 4 with full prompts available in the Appendix.
(1)
Candidate Generation. Using an LLM, we automatically rephrase individual reasons for preference annotations or general statements of values into one or more correctly formatted and generally applicable principles. This step is necessary as many human-written reasons or values are too narrow and specific (e.g., referring to a particular prompt), involve many semantically distinct concepts, or are simply written informally and idiomatically.
(2)
Clustering. We embed each candidate principle as a numerical vector using a sequence embedding model. We then cluster the resulting embedded candidates. Clustering serves two purposes: Deduplication of many repeated candidates and identification of broadly relevant themes.
(3)
Summarization. Using an LLM, we automatically summarize the most central candidates within each cluster (which often include somewhat different wordings of similar concepts) as new candidate principles.
(4)
Scoring and Selection. The reduced set of summarized candidates are scored, either by their ability to predict relevant preferences (for preference annotations with reasons) or by their centrality within the embedding space as a soft proxy for consensus (for general statements of values). The top scoring candidates (up to the desired number) are selected.
Outline and Contributions
(1)
Section 2 characterizes two kinds of principles: contextual and general. We argue that contextual principles should be grounded in reasons or justifications, and that general principles are also necessary to faithfully capture relevant value and concerns about alignment.
(2)
Section 3 surveys related work on alignment, principle elicitation, and evaluation criteria for constitutions.
(3)
Section 4 presents Grounded Constitutional AI (GCAI), the first unified framework for eliciting a constitution grounded in contextual and general human reasons and values written in natural language.
(4)
Section 5 discusses our evaluation methodology, including a discussion of the novel evaluation criteria we propose for constitutions.
(5)
Section 6 presents our main empirical results evaluating a constitution learned by GCAI compared to ICAI. Human survey participants overwhelmingly prefer the GCAI constitution across multiple evaluation dimensions, and we investigate the reasons for these preferences.
(6)
Section 7 presents qualitative and benchmark results of a model that we align to our the constitution learned by GCAI in comparison to that learned by ICAI. While the constitutions make little difference in benchmark performance, qualitatively we find that there are consistent thematic differences between the resulting models, with the GCAI-aligned model showing much more emphasis on ethics, safety, and non-discrimination.
(7)
Section 8 concludes with reflections on constitutional elicitation broadly based on our findings.
2. Grounding in Human Reasons and Values: Contextual and General Principles
We distinguish between two kinds of alignment principles the differ in their origin:
•
Contextual principles arise from actual interaction experience with models. They may depend heavily on the prompt distribution, pretraining, and fine-tuning of the particular model with which a human interacts.
•
General principles arise from anticipated concerns about hypothetical or possible model behavior. They represent prior commitments and do not depend on particular observed behaviors of a given LLM but rather on the broad values and concerns about possible LLM use.
Inverse Constitutional AI (ICAI) ( Findeis et al., 2025 ) tries to learn constitutional principles directly from preference annotations, a characteristic source for contextual principles. A human preference annotation includes a prompt, two example responses, and a selection of the preferred response. However, we emphasize that
principles are underdetermined by preference annotations , in the sense that a given preference annotation might be grounded in multiple unrelated or even conflicting reasons for that preference. For example, consider the following preference annotation drawn from the Helpsteer 2 Dataset ( Wang et al., 2024 ) .
Prompt
User: I have a flurk in my glooben!
Response 1
LLM: I’m sorry, I don’t speak whatever language that is. Can you please rephrase your concern in English? I’m here to help!
Response 2 (preferred ✓ \checkmark )
LLM: I’m here to help answer your questions and engage in positive, respectful, and ethical conversations. However, I’m afraid I don’t understand the terms “flurk” and “glooben.” Could you please provide more context or clarify what you mean? I’ll do my best to assist you once I have a better understanding of your question.
The user prompt uses nonsense words, and both responses politely express a need for clarification and a willingness to help. What might explain the preference for Response 2? Multiple plausible reasons come to mind that would result in very different candidate principles. For example, perhaps Response 2 is preferred because it is more complete and detailed, fully clarifying its intended purpose and precisely highlighting the exact terms it cannot interpret. While initially plausible, this would completely miss the mark of the actual annotator reasons.
Annotator’s Reasons:
Response 2 is slightly better than Response 1 because it asks questions in a considerate way…While both responses are polite, Response 2’s tone is more open and accommodating, reflecting a better alignment with the potential for creative or playful engagement suggested by the original prompt. The actual reasons serve to ground principles of openness and non-dismissiveness in tone, having nothing to do with a preference for a more detailed response. An LLM (or human, for that matter) attempting to derive principles from the preference annotations alone might come to entirely the wrong conclusion based on a spurious inference.
Contextual principles are invaluable as a source of nuance about style, tone, and complex interpretations of helpfulness. But they are also insufficient. In particular, principles to which the model is already well aligned will not surface regularly in contextual interaction. In other words, contextual principle elicitation is heavily biased by the model and prompt distribution used for collecting the relevant preference data. Related, principles regarding safety and harm that are rarely relevant to normal interaction (but represent critical risks in rare interactions), will be underemphasized.
We find evidence for this concern empirically by a comparative analysis of themes in the PRISM dataset ( Kirk et al., 2024 ) compared to the Helpsteer 2 Dataset ( Wang et al., 2024 ) . Specifically, we compare the human written reasons for preferences in the Helpsteer 2 dataset (the contextual case) with the general statements of alignment values contributed by human annotators in the PRISM survey data before and apart from their actual interactions with models (the general case). 1 1

3. Related Work
3.1. Alignment Techniques
Most alignment techniques directly fine-tune an LLM on a dataset of human feedback, typically human annotations of preference between paired examples of generations. Examples of such techniques include reinforcement learning from human feedback (RLHF) ( Christiano et al., 2017 ; Stiennon et al., 2020 ; Ouyang et al., 2022 ; Bai et al., 2022a ) , Direct Preference Optimization (DPO) ( Rafailov et al., 2023 ) , and its generalizations Ψ \Psi PO ( Azar et al., 2024 ) and GPO ( Tang et al., 2024 ) . Constitutional alignment ( Bai et al., 2022b ; Huang et al., 2024 ; Fränken et al., 2024 ; Findeis et al., 2025 ; Kyrychenko et al., 2025 ) differ by explicitly articulating a constitution: a set of principles expressed in natural language. The original Constitutional AI technique uses a combination of instruction-tuning, self-critique and revision, and reinforcement learning from AI feedback (RLAIF) to fine-tune a model given a constitution ( Bai et al., 2022b ) . Alternative techniques include supervised fine-tuning with AI-generated examples ( Sun et al., 2023 ) or conditional mutual information maximization ( Fränken et al., 2024 ) .
3.2. Alignment Goals and Learning from Stakeholder Input
Prior work has argued that the normative aspects of alignment should be confronted explicitly through a principle-based approach ( Gabriel, 2020 ) . Helpfulness, harmlessness, and honesty have emerged as leading contenders ( Askell et al., 2021 ; Bai et al., 2022a ; Ouyang et al., 2022 ) but may be too general and in need of interpretation to adequately inform model alignment. At a more detailed level, there is substantive disagreement over the relevant values and principles for alignment in a pluralistic society ( Wu et al., 2023 ; Sorensen et al., 2024b ; Sorensen et al., 2024a ) . For this reason, some have argued to focus on a fair process for determining alignment goals rather than a particular fixed set of principles ( Gabriel and Keeling, 2025 ) . Constitutional AI is promising insofar as the principles written in natural language are directly used for model alignment. This enables transparency and collective participation ( Groves et al., 2023 ; Suresh et al., 2024 ) in the alignment process apart from the provision of preference annotations for training black-box reward models. How then can we elicit constitutions from participating stakeholders?
Inverse Constitutional AI (ICAI) ( Findeis et al., 2025 ) attempts to learn principles inferred from human preference annotations. ICAI uses an LLM to generate conjectural principles that could explain a preference annotation, then scores the resulting principles by their ability to broadly predict the preference dataset as a whole. In the language of GCAI, this amounts to learning contextual principles from preference annotations without reasons. Huang et al. (2024) proposed Collective Constitutional AI, wherein participants propose principles directly and then vote on a subset of the candidate principles ( Huang et al., 2024 ) . This approach focuses on general principles. In contrast, GCAI learns both general principles directly from human statements of values and contextual principles principles from preference annotations corroborated by human-written reasons or justifications for those preferences, disambiguating and reducing the reliance on conjectural LLM interpretation of preferences.
3.3. Evaluating Alignment Principles
Most alignment projects focus on human preference evaluation of the aligned model or automated benchmarks such as AlpacaEval ( Dubois et al., 2024 ) or Arena-Hard-Auto ( Li et al., 2024 ) . While we do align models to our constitution and evaluate standard reasoning ( Hendrycks et al., 2021b ) and bias ( Parrish et al., 2022 ) benchmarks, we also seek to directly evaluate the constitution or principles themselves that are the immediate output artifact of GCAI and related techniques like ICAI. We draw from a landscape of three distinct sources to identify evaluation dimensions: foundational political theory, contemporary constitutional design, and AI-specific constitutional evaluation. In particular, the principles outlined by legal philosopher Lon Fuller’s in his seminal The Morality of Law are incorporated into our criteria of Generality , Clarity , and Coherence ( Fuller, 1969 ) . We also draw upon John Rawl’s concept of Public Reason, in which he posits that a justifiable constitution must be acceptable to all over which it holds authority, to evaluate with respect to Fairness and Consensus ( Larmore, 2002 ) . We also consider contemporary frameworks for constitutional design, such as that proposed by Nworka and Hedling, particularly as they focus on applications, from which we draw the dimensions of Feasibility , Constancy , and Faithfulness ( Nwokora, 2022 ) , ( Hedling, 2011 ) . Finally, we turn to literature that examine constitutions specifically as they relate to artificial intelligence. Although Moral Grounding of constitutions is emphasized across scholarship, it is of particular emphasis in Mei and Broyde’s ( Mei and Broyde, 2025 ) framework of covenantal authority as a touchstone for constitutional evaluation vis-à-vis artificial intelligence. We expand on these evaluative criteria in Section 5
4. Elicitation Process
The unified framework for eliciting contextual and general principles follows a five-stage structure: 1) Candidate generation , 2) Clustering , 3) Summarization , 4) Scoring and Selection . Figure 1 illustrates how certain stages employ different methods depending on the dataset. In this section, we outline the implementation of each stage for both contextual and general principle elicitation.

4.1. Candidate Generation
For the contextual principles, we use a subset of the HelpSteer2 ( Wang et al., 2024 ) dataset. We then use the model gpt-4.1-mini-2025-04-14 and the prompt in Appendix C.1 to infer candidate principles from the justification text, as in the following example:
Prompt:
I want you to act as an explainer and go in depth about a topic.
Response 1:
Sure, I can help. What topic would you like me to explain in depth?
Response 2:
Sure, I would be happy to help explain a topic in depth. What topic would you like me to explain?
Some things to keep in mind as I am explaining a topic: I will use simple language and avoid technical jargon as much as possible; I will provide examples and analogies to help make the topic more relatable and understandable; I will break down complex concepts into smaller, more manageable pieces; and I will provide a clear and concise summary of the topic at the end.
Let me know what topic you would like me to explain, and I will do my best to provide a thorough and understandable explanation.
Preference justification:
Response 2 is slightly better than Response 1.
Helpfulness: Response 2 provides a more structured and detailed plan for explaining the topic, making it slightly more helpful than Response 1, which lacks specificity.
Clarity: Response 2 presents a more coherent and clear outline of how the topic will be explained, reducing confusion.
Generated principles:
Provide a clear and detailed plan or outline to enhance helpfulness; use structured and specific information to improve clarity and reduce confusion.
This exemplifies how the justification adds context and value to the preference, allowing the LLM to extract or infer principles that better align with the reasons why the user preferred one response, rather than simply inferring them from the preference label alone.
For the general principles, we use the free-text answers from PRISM ( Kirk et al., 2024 ) that answer the question of which set of principles stakeholders think AI should follow, independent of what task it is performing. These responses were not single isolated statements, but descriptions of values that often expressed multiple distinct principles. To obtain individual principle candidates, we decompose each constitution into a set of principles by feeding a structured prompt and few-shot examples to the gpt-4.1-2025-04-14 model (See § C.2 ). The resulting decompositions can be seen in the following example:
Stakeholder-Written Constitution:
Be friendly and uplifting in conversation. Do not show me any vile or unethical responses. Remember past conversations and learn from them what I like and don’t like. Always be respectful.
Decomposed principles:
AI should be friendly and uplifting in conversation; AI should not provide vile or unethical responses; AI should remember past conversations and learn user preferences.
In this example, we can see that some values arise that would not likely be observed during the interaction of a user with a previously aligned LLM, given that such models are already tuned not to provide vile or unethical responses.
4.2. Clustering
The initial list of candidate principles is embedded using OpenAI’s text-embedding-3-small model 2 2
2
The specific choice of embedding model is not critical, as any model with comparable semantic similarity performance would be suitable. .
For contextual principles, we use hierarchical clustering to group similar embeddings based on cosine similarity. Compared to the k k -means clustering used in ICAI, hierarchical clustering better preserves unique principles, since k k -means requires the number of clusters K K to be fixed in advance. Because the true number of distinct principles generated in the first stage is unknown, specifying K K is difficult: if K K is too large, de-duplication is ineffective, and if K K is too small, unrelated principles are forced together. Hierarchical clustering instead allows us to specify a similarity threshold 3 3
3
We found 0.42 0.42 to be appropriate in our experiments in the sequence embedding space, rather than a fixed number of clusters.
When principles originate from stakeholder-written constitutions, we instead apply proportionally fair clustering ( Chen et al., 2019 ) . In this setting, the objective is not only to remove redundancy but also to ensure that different value groups expressed in the data remain represented in the resulting set of clusters. Note that this is appropriate for the PRISM survey data where humans directly contribute constitutions and can be seen as represented by their contribution. By contrast, we do not recommend proportionally fair clustering for contextual principles because the distribution is strongly biased by the prompt distribution human annotators considered (i.e., as an annotator you may have been given prompts that did not reflect your most serious concerns).
The maximal number of clusters is chosen based on the assumption that each proportionally fair cluster should represent at least three data points, which is consistent with the fairness assumptions of the method while still allowing for a relatively fine-grained representation of human values. For each such cluster, the most central principle is selected as the one whose embedding lies closest to the cluster centroid, following the representative-selection procedure of ( Chen et al., 2019 ) .
After clustering, we apply an initial de-duplication step using hierarchical clustering, as above, to merge clusters that are extremely similar in embedding space, reducing trivial redundancy while preserving proportional representation.
4.3. Summarization
To generate a list of de-duplicated principles, we prompt an LLM ( gpt-4.1-2025-04-14 ) to summarize the central principles within each cluster. We compute the mean embedding of all principles in a cluster and select the five nearest principle embeddings, which are then summarized. This deviates from ICAI, where a single principle is randomly selected from each cluster. Candidate principles within a given cluster tend to focus on a central idea, with slight variation in their precise wording. Summarizing a subset of these principles helps to faithfully represent more of the values present in a cluster 4 4
4
On the other hand, summarizing the entire cluster, for large clusters, resulted in some overly long principles which simply enumerated the details from the individual items within a cluster. .
4.4. Scoring and Selection
During scoring for contextual principles we consider how accurately candidate principles predict the original preference annotations. For each candidate principle and each annotation (prompt, two responses, and a preference), we prompt an LLM to select the response that better conforms to the given principle, with the option to abstain when the principle is irrelevant. A principle’s accuracy is computed as the number of times it correctly predicts the human preference when relevant, divided by the total number of relevant annotations plus a smoothing factor α \alpha 5 5
5
We use α = 9 \alpha=9 , proportional to the dataset size, to penalize principles that are extremely rarely relevant. .
This scoring procedure is not applicable to principles derived from stakeholder-written constitutions, since these are not grounded in response-level preference data and therefore cannot be evaluated by their ability to predict pairwise response choices.
Therefore, we instead compute a mean squared distance (MSD) score for each cluster and rank clusters by this score, which provides a notion of internal agreement within a cluster and thus serves as a proxy for consensus over the represented principle. Because some clusters may still express closely related concepts, we perform a final de-duplication step using hierarchical clustering 6 6
6
We use a lower similarity threshold of 0.3 to conservatively merge only near-identical principles while retaining semantically distinct ones. , merging semantically equivalent clusters and keeping the cluster with the lowest MSD as the representative.
Finally, we form a constitution by selecting the top K / 2 K/2 principles from each of the two elicitation sources, where K K is the desired size. For ease of evaluation we use a value K = 10 K=10 in our experiments, though in practice one may wish to use a much larger value of K K .

We updated the models to use the same model for principle generation ( gpt-4.1-mini-2025-04-14 ) and embedding ( text-embedding-3-small ) as our method. We used the same data for both algorithms 7 7

5.2. Evaluative Framework
Our framework for evaluation was informed by previous AI constitution research ( Mei and Broyde, 2025 ) , contemporary literature on constitutional design ( Hedling, 2011 ; Nwokora, 2022 ) , and foundational legal and political theory ( Fuller, 1969 ; Larmore, 2002 ) .

This framework is designed to engage in three distinct assessments: legitimacy , conceptual integrity , and applicability . The first set of criteria answers the meta-question, "Why should the system be bound by these rules?" as part of addressing the question of credibility and legitimacy. One source is its moral grounding , a foundational criterion that threads previous literature, both canonical and contemporary. For example, Lon Fuller notes in The Morality of Law that "legality is not a matter of form alone, but of fidelity to a moral enterprise." ( Fuller, 1969 ) Moral grounding as an evaluative dimensions, thus, challenges whether principles and constitutions are anchored in moral traditions that inculcate values-driven standards.
Political philosopher John Rawls, in his concept of Public Reason ( Larmore, 2002 ) , argues that justifiable constitutions must also be acceptable to all of its constituents, a position we capture in the dimensions of fairness and consensus .
The criteria of generality , clarity , and coherence assess conceptual integrity, the logical and semantic quality of principles and constitutions. In other words, they pose the question, "Are the principles (and constitutions) well-designed to guide behavior?" Generality addresses whether principles bear adequate conceptual breadth for situational applications and offer an architecture for predictable decision-making. Clarity assesses whether a principle can be meaningfully interpreted; it counterweights generality in ensuring that abstractions still offer understandable instruction. Finally, coherence measures at a constitution level the assurance of cogency such that principles can co-exist without significant conflict.
Finally, this evaluative framework asks, "Do these standards hold water in real-world applications?" The prima facie criterion here is feasibility , which examines how principles might intersect with technological, social, and economic constraints. With AI safety in mind, we raise an additional test of faithfulness , taking into account how human- or machine-based actions may distort the intent of a principle for malicious purposes. Finally, this framework considers constancy , a resistance to temporal brittleness, which cautions against transient assumptions encoded into principles written today and anticipates how shifting contexts may invalidate principles in ways orthogonal to original moral intent, logic, and application.
5.3. Survey Methodology
We evaluated constitutions generated by both algorithms through two user surveys: 1) constitution-level, and 2) principle-level. 101 participants were recruited through the Prolific platform and randomly assigned the one of the two surveys. Our protocol was approved by our institutional review board (IRB) and all materials are included in Appendix F .
51 participants completed the constitution-level survey. These participants were shown both constitutions (in randomized order) (See Figure 2 and Figure 3 in Appendix A ). We first asked participants to indicate which constitution they would prefer both 1) personally, and 2) for governing AI behavior for the U.S. population. After each of these questions we also asked participants to elaborate on what factors informed their preference in free text. Lastly, we asked participants to rate the constitutions along three dimensions: 1) moral grounding , 2) consensus , and 3) coherence on a 5-point Likert scale.
The remaining 50 participants completed the principle-level survey. Participants were randomly shown six individual principles, three from each of the two constitutions. First, they were asked if they personally agreed with the principle, and if the principle would be appropriate for governing AI behavior for the general U.S. population. They were then asked to evaluate each principle according to its: 1) moral grounding , 2) fairness , 3) generality , 4) clarity , 5) feasibility , 6) constancy , and 7) faithfulness . Participants indicated on a five-point Likert scale their level of agreement that the principle embodied each dimension.
5.4. Aligned Model Evaluation
We aligned a based pretrained Mistral-7B ( Jiang et al., 2023 ) model to the principles from both the GCAI constitution and the ICAI constitution we generated. We used the Constitutional AI (CAI) ( Bai et al., 2022b ) framework using principle-guided critique, revision, and preference-based optimization. However, we used DPO ( Rafailov et al., 2023 ) for the fine-tuning with AI-generated preference feedback, while ( Bai et al., 2022b ) used RLHF (see § B for full details).
For evaluating the aligned models, we sampled 100 red-teaming prompts from the Babelscape/ALERT ( Tedeschi et al., 2024 ) dataset, and generated responses with both the ICAI and GCAI finetuned models (200 responses total). These responses were qualitatively analyzed by researchers to identify differences between the ICAI and GCAI finetuned models (See § 5.5 ). We opted not to submit these generations to crowdworker survey participants out of ethical concern, as several of these red-teaming prompts are highly toxic and sensitive (See § G ).
We also evaluate whether alignment to different constitutions has an effect on the models’ language understanding capabilities as well as their social biases. We benchmark on MMLU ( Hendrycks et al., 2021a ) to measure general multi-domain language understanding, and Social Bias BBQ ( Parrish et al., 2022 ) to test whether models exhibit stereotyping under ambiguous and disambiguated social contexts (See § 7.1 ).
5.5. Qualitative Data Analysis
We conducted qualitative data analysis of the free responses collected in the constitution survey, and the responses generated by our finetuned models. For both analyses researchers double coded a sample of responses (38 and 32 for the constitution survey and finetuned model generations, respectively) to establish an initial code book. Researchers then met to resolve any disagreements between their code books and consolidate a single set of agreed upon themes. The remaining data was then coded individually by researchers. No new themes emerged in the constitution survey data, however three new themes emerged while coding the finetuned model generations. Researchers recoded all previous responses to consider the new themes as they emerged (See § 6.1 , and § 7.2 ).
