GCAI is more frequently associated with safety- and norm-oriented categories, including harm reduction or redirection, ethical prompting, harmless resources and advice, and physical or mental health and safety. It also shows higher rates of anti-discrimination and anti-misinformation framing. In contrast, ICAI is more often coded as producing harmful or violent suggestions, mis- or disinformation and discriminatory content.
8. Discussion
8.1. Constitutions Are More Than The Sum of Their Parts
When evaluating standalone principles from the GCAI and ICAI constitutions, participants expressed little preference for principles from one constitution over the other (See § 6.6 ). This was not the case when participants viewed the constitutions holistically. In a head-to-head comparison of constitutions, participants preferred the GCAI constitutions on all evaluation dimensions (See § 6.1 ). This highlights an underappreciated dynamic of constitutions for AI alignment: that the synergistic composition of a constitution is an important factor in it’s approval from stakeholders. To further illustrate this point, we note that while factuality was the most important factor in making constitution-level preferences (See 3 ), it was evaluated similarly to other principles in the principle-level evaluation (See 14 ).
8.2. Constitutions from GCAI Are Only Candidates and Should Be Discussed and Ratified
GCAI is notably a framework for eliciting candidate constitutions from stakeholder reasons and values. GCAI is designed to generate constitutions grounded in the values of a stakeholder population, which could reasonably garner widespread support. While the GCAI framework employs various scoring metrics during final principle selection, these metrics are far removed from direct human input, and are applied to principles that stakeholders have never actually seen. These scoring metrics should not be interpreted as valid expressions of support from stakeholders. Crucially GCAI does not have a method for ratifying the constitutions it generates. Before employing a GCAI constitution for model alignment developers should verify with relevant stakeholders that the constitution accurately reflects the pluralistic values of the population.
8.3. Justifications Increase Transparency and Faithfulness
One of the benefits described in standard ICAI ( Findeis et al., 2025 ) is the ability to better interpret the principles guiding a preference annotation dataset. By incorporating justifications into our principle generation pipeline we further increase the transparency of preference data by more faithfully adhering to the true underlying reasoning of the human annotators. One limitation described by the original ICAI authors is that multiple constitutions may explain data equally well, so ICAI cannot claim to surface the exact principles used by the original data annotators. While this remains a limitation of our approach (and is, we believe, an inherent limitation in inferring principles from annotation data) we believe that incorporating justifications allows GCAI to more closely reflect the principles used during the original annotation task.
Limitations and Future Work
In this work we combine human reasons and values data from two different datasets. In practice GCAI is meant to elicit both general and contextual principles from the same stakeholder population. Future work should validate GCAI in more realistic deployment settings with a unified data source and large scale deployment for testing.
LLMs are used for generation and summarization within GCAI. While grounding candidate in the justifications and values written explicitly improves faithfulness, GCAI cannot guarantee perfect faithfulness and is subject to any biases of the LLM used within the technique.
Additionally, while GCAI generates constitutions of principles, the technique itself does not automatically guarantee the appropriateness of every principle that may be generated. In addition, no technique can guarantee perfect representation of every input perspective when multiple stakeholders disagree. Thus the final results require human oversight. As importantly, the final results require discussion and ratification from the relevant stakeholders for any given deployment. Future work should 1) investigate stakeholder attitudes towards GCAI constitutions, and 2) formalize a fair ratification process that incorporates feedback from the entire stakeholder population.

Appendix B Alignment Procedure
B.1. Supervised Learning Dataset Construction
The dataset creation follows the same methodology introduced in CAI ( Bai et al., 2022b ) . First, 2000 prompts were sampled from the Babelscape/ALERT ( Tedeschi et al., 2024 ) dataset, which is specifically designed to elicit undesirable or unsafe behavior. These prompts form the basis for generating initial model responses that the model later critiques and revises.
For the generation of the critiques and revision, the model mistral-instruct-v0.1 was selected. This model is instruction-tuned but does not contain excessive safety layers or restrictive guardrails, which makes it similar to the model used in CAI ( Bai et al., 2022b ) , a model that is primarily helpful, rather than strongly safety-constrained.
Given a prompt, an initial response is generated using the model, after which a randomly selected principle from the constitution is applied. The procedure consists of three stages: (1) generating an initial answer, (2) generating a critique conditioned on a principle, and (3) producing a revised answer. The following prompt templates were used.
